## Lesson Overview
- **Topic:** Chapter 11: Light: Shadows and Reflections
- **Grade:** Grade 7
- **Subject:** Science
- **Duration:** 40-45 minutes
- **CBSE Unit:** Chapter 11: Light: Shadows and Reflections (straight-line travel of light, shadows, reflection and images)

## Learning Objectives
By the end of this lesson, students will be able to:
1. Classify materials as transparent, translucent or opaque based on how much light passes through them, and explain how a shadow forms.
2. Describe the properties of the image formed by a plane mirror (erect, same size, laterally inverted, not obtained on a screen).
3. Explain, using the straight-line travel of light, why a pinhole camera forms an inverted image, and compare this with a plane-mirror image.

## Prerequisites
Students should already know:
- The difference between luminous objects (which give out their own light, such as the Sun) and non-luminous objects (which are seen by reflected light, such as the Moon).
- That a torch, candle or lamp is a common everyday source of light.

## Materials & Resources
- NCERT Textbook Grade 7 Science
- Blackboard / Whiteboard
- A torch, a small plane mirror, and samples of cardboard, tracing paper and glass/plastic sheet (or similar transparent/translucent/opaque items) if available
- Chart paper/notebook for a comparison table
- OPTIONAL: projector to show textbook figures of Activities 11.4, 11.7 and 11.9 if physical materials or a working pinhole camera are not available

## Lesson Plan (Step-by-Step)

### Introduction & Hook (5 minutes)
- Shine a torch (or describe doing so) at the wall and ask: "If I hold up my notebook, a sheet of glass, and a piece of tracing paper one at a time in front of the torch, will the light pass through each one in the same way?" Take 2-3 predictions.
- Tell students that today's lesson explores how light behaves when it meets different materials, mirrors, and a simple pinhole camera - all based on one key idea: light travels in a straight line.

### Direct Instruction (15 minutes)
- Chunk 1 - Materials and shadows: Explain the three categories: transparent materials let almost all light pass through, translucent materials let only part of the light pass, and opaque materials block light almost completely. Explain that a shadow forms when an opaque object blocks light from reaching a surface, and that a source of light, an object, and a screen are all needed to see a shadow (Activity 11.4). Ask: "If I move the object closer to the torch but keep the torch and screen fixed, what happens to the shadow's size?" (It becomes larger, because the object blocks a wider spread of the rays.)
- Chunk 2 - Reflection and mirror images: Explain that when light hits a shiny surface like a mirror, its direction changes - this is called reflection. Describe Activity 11.7: an object held before a plane mirror produces an image that is the same size as the object and stays upright (erect), but the image cannot be captured on a screen placed behind or in front of the mirror. Ask: "If I write my name on paper and hold it up to a mirror, will it look exactly the same?" (No - it will appear laterally inverted, left and right reversed.)
- Chunk 3 - Pinhole camera: Explain that in a pinhole camera, light from an object passes through a tiny hole and forms an image on a screen behind it (Activity 11.9). Because light travels in straight lines, rays from the top of the object cross at the pinhole and land on the lower part of the screen, and rays from the bottom land on the upper part - so the image is upside down (inverted). Ask: "Is this inversion the same as the lateral inversion we saw in the mirror?" (No - the pinhole camera flips the image top-to-bottom; the mirror flips it left-to-right.)

### Guided Practice (10 minutes)
- As a class, sort a list of everyday materials (glass, cardboard, tracing paper, cloth curtain, aluminium foil, thin plastic sheet) into transparent, translucent and opaque columns on the board, with students explaining their reasoning for at least two items each.
- Then, working in pairs, students complete a short comparison chart in their notebooks: "Plane mirror image" vs "Pinhole camera image" - same size or not, erect or inverted, type of inversion (lateral vs top-to-bottom), and whether it can be captured on a screen. Review answers together and correct any confusion between the two types of inversion.

### Student Activity (10 minutes)
- In pairs, students use a small plane mirror to test lateral inversion: they write their own first name in large letters on paper, hold it up facing the mirror, and sketch what they observe in the mirror in their notebook, labelling which letters look the same and which look reversed.
- Pairs then predict, in one sentence, what would happen to the same written name if it were viewed through a working pinhole camera instead of a mirror, based on today's lesson.

### Assessment & Closure (5 minutes)
- Quick formative check 1: Ask a student to classify glass, cardboard and tracing paper as transparent, translucent or opaque.
- Quick formative check 2: Ask what happens to a shadow's size when the object moves closer to the light source.
- Quick formative check 3: Ask a student to state one property of a plane-mirror image (same size / erect / laterally inverted / not obtained on a screen).
- Brief summary: shadows form when opaque objects block light; plane mirrors give erect, laterally inverted images; pinhole cameras give inverted images on a screen - all because light travels in a straight line.
- Exit ticket: "A ball is placed between a torch and a screen. Is the shadow formed opaque, translucent, or does no shadow form? Explain your answer using the idea of blocked light."

## Homework Assignment
- At home, find one transparent, one translucent and one opaque object. Write down each object's name and briefly explain, in your own words, why it belongs in that category based on how light passes through it.

## Differentiation Strategies
- **For students needing additional support:** Provide a simple word bank (transparent, translucent, opaque, erect, laterally inverted, inverted) to use when completing the Guided Practice sorting and comparison chart. Give a partially filled mirror-vs-pinhole comparison chart with one row already completed as a model. Allow support-needing pairs to describe their mirror observation orally before writing it down.
- **For students ready for extension:** Ask students to explain, using straight-line travel of light, how a periscope (two plane mirrors in a Z-shaped box) allows someone to see over an obstacle, and to sketch the path of one light ray through it. Alternatively, ask them to justify why letters like "T" and "O", which are symmetrical top-to-bottom, look the same in a mirror while most other letters do not.

## Common Misconceptions to Address
1. Misconception: A shadow is a black copy that shows every detail of the object's colour and pattern. Correction: a shadow is simply the region receiving less or no direct light because the object blocked it; the object's colour does not determine the shadow's colour.
2. Misconception: A plane mirror turns the image upside down. Correction: a plane mirror keeps the image erect (right-side up) but produces lateral inversion (left-right reversal); only the pinhole camera produces a genuinely inverted (upside-down) image.
3. Misconception: The Moon is a source of its own light. Correction: the Moon is non-luminous and is visible only because it reflects sunlight.

## NCERT Alignment
- Grade 7 Science, Chapter 11: Light: Shadows and Reflections. This lesson draws directly on the chapter's Activities 11.3/11.4 (transparent/translucent/opaque materials and shadow formation), Activity 11.7 (plane-mirror image properties) and Activity 11.9 (pinhole camera and inverted images).
